2. The facts as alleged in the plaint, in short, are that the suit land comprising of 182.23 acre described in Tauji No.10 of the then Mymensingh Collectorate originally belonged to Zamindar Haider Ali Khan Panni and others and the same having formed the saham of Haider Ali Khan Panni was accordingly recorded in his name in the CS khatian. The suit land along with other land constituted a waqf estate and Haider Ali Khan Panni himself was appointed as Mutawalli. During his tenure as Mutawalli Haider Ali Khan Panni settled a total of 126.54 acre land out of the waqf estate with his two sons, namely, Mehdi Ali Khan Panni and Sayeed Ali Khan Panni, and his two grandsons, namely Bayezid Khan Panni and Daud Khan Panni by executing a Jote-Pattannama in the year 1353 BS and handed over possession to them. The lessees having taken pattan of the land as above had been enjoying the same by paying rent to the Zamindari Estate. Meanwhile, SA operation started in the area and except a portion of land that was earlier transferred by the lessees rest 118.34 acre was recorded in their joint names. Thus the lessees and their heirs, as the case may be, had been in peaceful possession and enjoyment of the land in the suit khatian by paying rent to the Government. 

 4. The Government as defendant No.9 contested the suit by filing a written statement. The simple case of the contesting defendant is that the suit land along with other lands was non-retainable khas land of the Zamindars. After the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, hereinafter referred to as the "SA&T Act, 1950" came into force the entire waqf estate in question was acquisitioned as non-retainable khas land as per the provisions of the said Act. After acquisition the same vested in the Government free from all encumbrances and was accordingly recorded in the name of the Government in its khas khatian. The alleged pattannama in the names of the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiff is forged, fabricated and subsequently created for the purpose of the suit. The original Zamindars did neither give settlement of the land to nor did they receive rent from anyone in respect of the suit land or the estate. Thus no right title and interest was created by the so-called pattannama allegedly executed in favour of the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiff. By the same token no right, title or interest was created in favour of the plaintiff by the subsequent sale deeds executed by the so-called pattanholders. The registered sale deeds under which title to the suit land is claimed are collusive, void and not acted upon passing no title or interest whatsoever in favour of the plaintiff. 

 5. The waqf estate being so taken over by the Government as non-retainable khas land of the rent-receivers the same vested in the Government as per law and it had no reason to and indeed never realized rent from anyone claiming under the Zamindars, be that he is a pattanholder or subsequent purchaser. The plaintiff and his predecessors-in-interest have althrough been aware of the acquisition and record of rights standing in the name of the Government in its khas khatain. Government while in possession of the suit estate in khas settled 5.43 acre land from plot No. 3183 of the suit khatian with the defendant No.1 in connection with Settlement Case No. 16/1 (XII) 84-85 and handed over possession of the same to him. Accordingly he has been in possession of the land on its southern side. The suit is, therefore, liable to be dismissed. 

 6. The suit was for declaration of title simpliciter in respect of a piece of land admittedly forming part of the waqf estate sought on the basis of purchase from a number of persons whose title in the land rested in pattan-settlement allegedly taken from the Mutawalli of the said waqf estate. Learned Subordinate Judge tried the suit on six issues and finally dismissed the same. The issues framed are as follows: 

 7. The issues framed suggest that there was no issue framed on the crucial question of the authority of the Mutawalli to give such perpetual pattan settlement of the waqf estate or any part thereof. No issue is found either on another crucial question ie, whether the waqf estate was acquisitioned by the Government as per provisions of the SA&T Act, 1950. And, if so, whether the rent-receiver had any subsisting saleable interest in the estate after acquisition. 

 9. The pattannama itself on a glance does not inspire satisfaction of the court about its genuineness. One Md. Abdul Halim is examined as PW.4 who claimed himself as Tahshilder of the Waqf Estate. He is 78 years of age. He is examined for proving the pattannama. He identified the handwriting of one Kanailal Sarkar who is styled as Pradhan Karjakarak (Chief Executive). There is nothing more about said Kanailal. Nevertheless, PW.4 claims that the pattannama was written by Kanailal and he is acquainted with and identified the handwriting of Kanailal. He sought to prove the mutation in the name of the plaintiff effected in 1996 and said that one Mannan Naib did the mutation. There is nothing about the whereabouts of said Mannan Naib. None of the attesting witnesses of the pattannama was examined. There is no explanation either about non-examination of Abdul Mannan. There is no explanation how the huge estate survived the acquisition by the Government so as to empower the Zamindars to receive rent from raiyats or pattan-holders. More importantly, not a single contemporaneous dakhila against the pattan was produced in court except one of 1996 which is again suspected by the trial court as fabricated and indeed seems to be so created for the purpose of the suit. A pattannama sought to be proved by a single dakhila showing payment of rent in the Zamindari sherista 54 years after the pattan-settlement that too when the estate had already stood acquisitioned, as would transpire herein later, can hardly be credited with truth. So is the case with statements made by the supporting witnesses examined by the plaintiff. 

 11. Mr. Abul Quasem, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant submits that the appellant has successfully proved its title and possession in the suit land. The 11 registered deeds by which the land is purchased was duly proved as Exhibit 3 and 7 Series. Mr. Quasem added that the plaintiff company mutated its name in respect of the suit land and has been paying rent. During the current survey operation the draft khatian of the land has been prepared in its name to the extent of 7.00 acres wrongly leaving aside rest 0.65½ acre. A settlement appeal is also filed by the plaintiff against the wrong recording. So far as the title of the plaintiff's predecessors is concerned Mr. Quasem submits that the suit land along with other land belonged to Karatia Zamindari Estate recorded in CS khatian No. 309 in the name of Zamindar Haider Ali Khan Panni. Haider Ali Khan Panni gave jote-settlement in 1350 BS of the entire 182.23 acre land of the estate to his two sons and two grandsons as is stated in the plaint and handed over possession. Accordingly SA and RS records were made in their names. They having thus taken settlement of the land possessed the same by paying rent to the Estate. The CS and RS khatians, draft khatian, mutation khatian of the Zamindari Estate and rent receipts are duly proved in court in support of the continuous and unbroken chain of title of the plaintiff. 

 12. The second branch of argument advanced by Mr. Abdul Quasem is that the predecessors-in-title of the plaintiff took settlement long before the East Bengal Sate Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, came into being. Moreover, the plaintiff's predecessors were not rent receivers. It follows therefore, that the gazette notification under section 43(2) dated 13-3-1975 seeking to acquire the rent receiving interest of the Estate has no manner of application to this case and it has not affected the right title and interest of the plaintiff in the suit land. 

 14. Mr. Gautam Kumar Roy learned Deputy Attorney General appearing on behalf of the Respondent No. 9 raised basically three contentions. He contended that law runs contrary to the power of Mutawalli in disposing of or creating charge or encumbrance on immoveable property held in waqf. The suit land, he insisted, is admittedly a part of a waqf estate, therefore, pattan, if any, given by the Mutawalli did not create any title or saleable interest in favour of the pattanholders. Mr. Roy next submits that the waqf estate was undeniably acquisitioned by the Government as "Haider Ali Khan Panni Wakf al-al-Aulad Estate" Karatia. The notification (Exhibit Gha), he insisted, issued under section 43(2) of the SA&T Act showing final stage of acquisition of the said estate was published in the official gazette dated 20-3-1975 which means abolition of any intermediate interest in the property or taking over by the Government non-retainable khas land to the extinction of saleable interest of the Zamindars and other land owners who turned into tenants under the state. He buttressed up his submission by reference to The Bangladesh (Legal Proceedings) (Third) Order, 1972 which bars, amongst others, suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings challenging the legality or validity of any provision of SA&T Act, 1950 or acquisition sought to be made therein. Mr. Roy finally submits that the question of law apart, the plaintiff miserably failed to prove the pattannama which is the only basis of its predecessor's title. 

 25. In the instant case title of the plaintiff is rooted into a piece of pattannama of 1343 BS by which its predecessors-in-title allegedly took settlement of the entire waqf estate from its Mutawalli. Put into the legal perspective as above the pattannama needs be tested in terms of its validity precisely for the reason that the plaintiff's case rises and falls with the fate of pattannama particularly in absence of any other case set out in its support. The pattannama allegedly executed by the Mutawalli himself, apart from the question of its genuineness, seeks to make permanent transfer by pattan the entire estate in favour of some of his descendants, ie, the vendors of the plaintiff. Legal position as examined above does not permit such permanent transfer of any waqf estate by any means to the total extinction of its basic purpose. It follows, therefore, that the pattan, if any, taken by the plaintiff's predecessors-in-title did not survive the period prescribed by law let alone creating any saleable interest in favour of them. 

 26. Besides the question of the transferability of waqf estate and credibility of the pattannama the most vital question that lingers through is whether the waqf estate survived the wholesale acquisition of rent receiving interest and non-retainable khas land under the SA & T Act, 1950? If the waqf estate is found to have vested in the Government by operation of law can the deeds create any right title or interest in favour of the plaintiff? 

 27. Wholesale acquisition of rent receiving interest and of the non-retainable khas land, for all practical purposes, started with the notifications issued under sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 3 of the SA&T Act, 1950 and passed through different phases until preparation and final publication of the compensation assessment rolls under section 42 of the Act. The interest of the rent receivers held under any waqf, waqf-al-al-aulad, debutter or other religious trust acquired under sub-section (1) or non-retainable khas land acquired under sub-section (2) of section 3 finally vested in the Government free from all encumbrances with the publication of the compensation assessment roll under section 42 and declaration about such publication under section 43(2) of the SA&T Act, 1950. Intermediate arrangements had to be made for administration and management specially of the land held in religious or other trust but not taken in possession by the Government till the date of commencement of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1960 by allowing the Mutawalli, shebait or trustee, as the case may be, to continue to manage such interest as the agent of the Government till the last day of the agricultural year in which notification under section 43(2) is published or till the Government exercises' its right of possession, whichever is later, After the deadline prescribed by law the Mutawalli ceased to have authority to manage the waqf estate even under the Government. From any point of view Mutawalli or the pattanholders under him cannot have any lawful claim of right or title in a waqf estate after completion of acquisition process with the declaration of final publication made under section 43(2) of the SA&T Act, 1950. 

 28. The suit land admittedly forms a portion of the "Haidar Ali Khan Panni Wakf al-al-Aulad Estate" Karatia. The single dakhila dated 25-2-1996 (Exhibit 6) sought to be proved by the plaintiff showing payment of rent in the Waqf Estate Karatia is issued by " Mohammad Haidar Ali Waqf al-al-aulad Estate," Karatia. The mutation order dated 28.11.1996 (Exhibit 5) proved by the plaintiff is also issued by the same Haidar Ali Waqf al-al-aulad Estate, Karatia. Mr. Abul Quasem, does not deny the fact that the suit property originally belonged to Karatia "Haidar Ali Khan Panni Wakf al-al-Aulad Estate." No dispute, therefore, is there about the identity of the suit land as part of the "Haidar Ali Khan Panni Waqf al-al-Aulad Estate." Karatia. 

 29. It is found from notification published in the official gazette dated 14-3-1975 (Exhibit Gha) published under section 43(2) of the SA& T Act, 1950, that the said "Haidar Ali Khan Panni Wakf al-al-Aulad Estate" Karatia, was acquisitioned as 'waqf estate' and that the compensation assessment roll in respect of the same was finally published as per section 42 of the Act meaning thereby that all formalities of acquisition of the waqf estate was complete with publication of notification as aforesaid finally vesting the estate in the Government free from all encumbrances. The rent-receiver or the land owner concerned after acquisition of his interest in his estate, tenure etc. or non-retainable khas land cannot have any subsisting saleable interest so as to transfer the same to anyone. It follows, therefore, that the sale deeds executed after acquisition of the estate did not create any right or title of the plaintiff in respect of the suit land.
